content: A back brace is a medical device specifically designed to restrict spinal motion in cases such as fractures or post-operative spinal fusions. By limiting spinal movement, the brace facilitates the healing process and reduces discomfort for the patient. There are two primary types of back braces commonly used: 1. Rigid Braces: These are custom-molded plastic devices that can restrict spinal motion by up to 50%. 2. Corset Braces: These are elastic braces that primarily limit forward spinal motion. They are often used to support spinal fusions or to provide additional support during activities that place stress on the spine, such as lifting heavy objects. Bracing for Scoliosis Back braces are frequently prescribed for the treatment of adolescent idiopathic scoliosis. These braces aim to halt the progression of spinal curvature in growing children. Several types of braces are used for this purpose, all of which are rigid and function by applying pressure to the existing curvature to prevent further progression. These braces are often custom-measured or molded by an orthotist or a clinical team. To protect the skin from irritation, a protective layer, such as a tank top or T-shirt, is typically worn underneath the brace. 1. Boston Brace: Made of molded plastic and usually worn under clothing. It can be removed for sports activities but is otherwise worn at all times. 2. Cervico-Thoraco-Lumbo-Sacral Orthosis (Milwaukee Brace): Similar in construction and use to the Boston brace but includes a neck ring to provide support for the cervical spine. 3. Charleston Brace: Designed to be worn only during sleep. It is molded to the patient while they are bent to the side, increasing pressure on the spinal curvature. Studies have shown that wearing this brace for 8 hours at night is as effective as wearing other braces for 23 hours a day. It is most effective for curvatures between 20 and 40 degrees, with the curve apex below the shoulder blade level. 4. SpineCor Brace: A flexible brace that allows freedom of movement and is less noticeable under clothing. It is typically worn for 20 hours a day. A bodysuit is recommended to be worn underneath. It is suitable for patients with a Cobb angle between 15 and 50 degrees. This newer design has shown positive results in a two-year follow-up study but is not recommended for patients with a Risser score above 3. 5. SPoRT Brace: A solid brace equipped with large sweeping pads (drives) to promote spinal elongation and stops to prevent incorrect movement relative to the curve. A key advantage is that it does not restrict limb movement. It is typically worn for 23 hours a day. 6. Chêneau Brace: Often used in conjunction with the Schroth Method of scoliosis rehabilitation. The brace features a shell padded with large sweeping pads and includes spaces that allow for patient movement. A modified version, the Lite Chêneau, replaces the bumped sections with open spaces for improved comfort and mobility.
